aboutThisFile.name: VJE sample document
aboutThisFile.purpose: Two jobs in one file: somewhere friendly to explore VJE for the first time, and the corpus VJE's own manual smoke tests are run against.
aboutThisFile.howToStart: Click any node in the Explorer tree on the left. The tabs on the right show that same node three ways -- Form, Text and Code. Everything here is editable: change something, then press Ctrl+Z to put it back.
aboutThisFile.howItIsLaidOut: The first few sections are ordinary data, so the application has something realistic to show. The sections after them are deliberate edge cases, each named for what it demonstrates.
goodPlacesToStart: planets -- select it to see an array drawn as a table
planets/0 -- select one element to see the same row as a form
application/window -- a small object, and the simplest thing to edit
strings/escapeSequences -- then change Settings > String display and watch it re-render
largeArray -- 2,000 elements, for when you want to see it stay responsive
aboutThisFile.youCannotBreakAnything: Nothing here is loaded by the application itself. Edit freely -- and if you save over it, git restores it.

arrayShapes._note: Every shape an array can take, and what VJE's array table does with each. Select the ARRAY (not an element) to see the table.

uniformObjects._note: The tidy case: same keys, same order, all scalars. This is what a table wants, and what CSV export was originally limited to.

raggedObjects._note: Members differ from element to element. The table shows the UNION of keys and leaves a cell empty where an element has no such member -- which is different from having it and it being null. Document > Normalize Array Elements fills the gaps with null, if that is what you want. CSV export writes the union too, with empty cells.

rows.name: delta
rows.comment: score is present here, and null -- compare with element 2, which has no score at all

scalarsOnly._note: No members to make columns from, so the table draws a single column headed by the array's own key.

mixedKinds._note: Elements of different kinds in one array. Legal JSON, and the same single-column rule applies.

withNestedContainers._note: Elements whose members are themselves containers. A cell that holds a container shows a placeholder -- {...} or [...] -- because a grid cell has one slot and a container has many. Drill into the element to edit what is inside. CSV export writes the same placeholder, and says how many cells it wrote that way.

arrayOfArrays._note: A matrix. Each element is an array, so each cell shows [...] and drilling in gives you the row.

empty._note: Nothing to draw. The table is empty, and CSV export refuses -- with a reason, on the menu item's tooltip.

growth._note: Move down past the last row and the table grows a provisional row (EDITOR-12). Type a value and it becomes real; move away without typing and it was never there. The object form does the same past its last field, materializing on the KEY (EDITOR-15).

scalarTypes._note: The six things a JSON value can be, at the top of the tree where they are easy to find.

numbers._note: VJE preserves each number's raw token exactly as it was written (FILE-10). Save the file and diff it -- none of these should have been rewritten into a different spelling of the same value.

strings._note: Everything a JSON string can carry. Settings > String display (Escaped / Decoded / Flattened) changes how the Form and Text views render these -- the Code View always shows the file's own notation.

escapeSequences._note: The eight two-character escapes JSON defines. In Escaped mode you see the backslash pairs; in Decoded mode you see what they mean; Flattened puts a multi-line value on one line.

lengths._note: Turn Settings > Wrap strings on and select this object in the Form view. Rows grow to hold their own value, and the ones beside them do not.
lengths.oneLine: A single line of ordinary prose, long enough to reach the edge of a narrow pane but not much further.
lengths.long: This value is deliberately long. It exists so that the Form view has something to wrap, the Text view has something to lay out under a hanging indent, and the printer has something to break across a page boundary at a width neither of them chose. Narrow the editor pane and it re-wraps; turn wrapping off and it elides instead.

lookalikes._note: Strings that look like other types. Each is a string here; retype one over a null cell and VJE reads the JSON literal you typed, so "42" without quotes becomes a number.

unicodeKeys._note: Keys are strings too, so anything a string can hold, a key can hold. These exercise the tree labels, the form's label column, Find, and Copy JSON Pointer.

emptyAndNull._note: The difference between absent, empty and null, which is easy to state and easy to lose.

jsonPointerEdgeCases._note: RFC 6901's own test cases. Select one, press Ctrl+Shift+C to copy its JSON Pointer, then Ctrl+G and paste it back -- Go To and Copy JSON Pointer are inverses, and these are the keys that make the escaping visible. A / inside a key is written ~1 in a pointer, and a ~ is written ~0.
jsonPointerEdgeCases: the empty string is a legal key -- its pointer ends with a bare slash
jsonPointerEdgeCases.a/b: a solidus inside a key; the pointer spells it ~1
a single space is a legal key all by itself
jsonPointerEdgeCases.m~n: a tilde inside a key; the pointer spells it ~0
jsonPointerEdgeCases.~1: a key that literally reads ~1 -- its pointer spells it ~01, which is the case that catches a naive unescape
jsonPointerEdgeCases.padded: leading and trailing spaces belong to the key. Go To deliberately does not trim what you type, because this key is real
jsonPointerEdgeCases.0: a key that looks like an array index, on an object
jsonPointerEdgeCases.-: a hyphen; on an ARRAY this would mean the position past the end

duplicateKeys._note: JSON allows duplicate sibling keys and VJE preserves them (FILE-04). It shows every one, and marks them all READ-ONLY on purpose: a JSON Pointer names only the FIRST member with a given key, so committing an edit to the second would silently write the first. Use Document > Rename Key to make one of them unique, and both become editable again. This is deliberate -- it is not a rendering fault.
duplicateKeys.unique: this one is editable, because nothing else shares its key

level_10.tryThis: Collapse Subtree on level_1, then Expand Subtree to bring it all back. Expand All and Collapse All are in the View menu and in the tree's own context menu.
level_10.siblingLeaf: a scalar beside the container, so the level is not all one kind

deepNesting._note: Ten levels, for Expand All / Collapse All and for the four expand/collapse commands. Each level carries a scalar beside the container so the tree has something to draw at every depth.
